title: Ἀνὴρ ἀδύνατα ἐπαγγελλόμενος
titleEn: The Man Who Promised the Impossible
part: The Man Who Promised the Impossible (Chambry 46 · Perry 34)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 46 (= Perry 34). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνὴρ πένης νοσῶν καὶ κακῶς διακείμενος, ἐπειδὴ ἀπὸ τῶν ἰατρῶν ἀπηλπίσθη, τοῖς θεοῖς ηὔχετο ἑκατόμβην ποιήσειν ἐπαγγελλόμενος καὶ ἀναθήματα καθιερώσειν, ἐὰν ἐξαναστῇ.
sentences.tr: Anēr penēs nosōn kai kakōs diakeimenos, epeidē apo tōn iatrōn apēlpisthē, tois theois ēucheto hekatombēn poiēsein epangellomenos kai anathēmata kathierōsein, ean exanastēi.
sentences.l: A poor man, being-ill and in a bad way, when by the doctors he was given-up, was praying to the gods, promising to make a hecatomb and to dedicate votive offerings, if he should get up again.
sentences.i: A poor man lay ill and in a bad way, and when the doctors had given him up he began praying to the gods, promising that he would offer a hecatomb and dedicate votive gifts if he got back on his feet.
sentences.n: ἀπηλπίσθη is passive — he was despaired of by the doctors. A ἑκατόμβη is nominally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; ἀναθήματα are objects set up in a sanctuary to discharge a vow. The two future infinitives (ποιήσειν, καθιερώσειν) are what a promise takes in Greek: 'undertaking that he would…'. ἐὰν ἐξαναστῇ, ἐάν with the subjunctive, is the ordinary future condition.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ γυναικὸς (ἐτύγχανε γὰρ αὐτῷ παρεστῶσα) πυνθανομένης· « Καὶ πόθεν αὐτὰ ἀποδώσεις ; » ἔφη· « Νομίζεις γάρ με ἐξαναστήσεσθαι, ἵνα καὶ ταῦτά με οἱ θεοὶ ἀπαιτήσωσιν ; »
sentences.tr: Tēs de gynaikos (etynchane gar autōi parestōsa) pynthanomenēs· « Kai pothen auta apodōseis ; » ephē· « Nomizeis gar me exanastēsesthai, hina kai tauta me hoi theoi apaitēsōsin ; »
sentences.l: And his wife (for she happened to be standing beside him) asking: « And from where will you pay these things? » he said: « Why, do you think I shall get up again, so that the gods should demand these things too from me? »
sentences.i: His wife — she happened to be standing by — asked: « And where will you find it all to pay? » « Why, » he said, « do you suppose I am going to recover, and have the gods come asking me for these as well? »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute wrapped round a parenthesis: τῆς γυναικὸς … πυνθανομένης, 'his wife asking'. ἐτύγχανε … παρεστῶσα is τυγχάνω with the supplementary participle — the main idea sits in the participle, 'happened to be standing by'. The joke is in the ἵνα clause: the vow costs him nothing, since he does not expect to live to be billed for it. Chambry prints the Greek question mark ; and spaces it away from the word, as French typography does.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ταῦτα ῥᾴδιον ἄνθρωποι κατεπαγγέλλονται ἃ τελέσειν ἔργῳ οὐ προσδοκῶσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti tauta rhāidion anthrōpoi katepangellontai ha telesein ergōi ou prosdokōsin.
sentences.l: The story shows that men easily promise those things which they do not expect to carry out in deed.
sentences.n: ῥᾴδιον is the neuter adjective doing duty as an adverb, 'easily'. ἔργῳ, 'in deed', is the standing opposite of λόγῳ, 'in word' — the whole fable folded into one dative.
